questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a performance deficiency of an overloaded aircraft?
distractors: Higher stalling speed
Longer takeoff run
Reduced rate and angle of climb
questions.explanation: The chapter lists 'Reduced maneuverability' as a deficiency of an overloaded aircraft, not increased maneuverability. Higher stalling speed, longer takeoff run, and reduced rate and angle of climb are all explicitly listed as performance deficiencies.

reference.text: The most important performance deficiencies of an overloaded aircraft are: Higher takeoff speed, Longer takeoff run, Reduced rate and angle of climb, Lower maximum altitude, Shorter range, Reduced cruising speed, Reduced maneuverability, Higher stalling speed, Higher approach and landing speed, Longer landing roll, Excessive weight on the nose wheel or tail wheel

questions.question: A pilot reduces the fuel load to lower the aircraft's weight during flight planning. What consequence must be taken into consideration?
questions.correct_answer: The range of the airplane will decrease
distractors: The CG will shift forward proportionally
The aircraft's structural integrity will be compromised
The stalling speed will increase
questions.explanation: The chapter states that reducing fuel to lower weight results in a decrease in range that must be considered. The CG does not necessarily shift forward proportionally, structural integrity is not compromised by reducing weight, and stalling speed would decrease, not increase, with lower weight.

reference.text: If a pilot lowers airplane weight by reducing fuel, the resulting decrease in the range of the airplane must be taken into consideration during flight planning.

questions.section: Balance, Stability, and Center of Gravity
questions.question: The center of gravity (CG) of an aircraft is best described as:
questions.correct_answer: The point at which the aircraft would balance if it were suspended at that point
distractors: The fixed point at which the aircraft's lift is concentrated
The geometric center of the wing's mean aerodynamic chord
The location of the reference datum established by the manufacturer
questions.explanation: The chapter defines CG as the point at which the aircraft would balance if suspended at that point. It is not fixed (it shifts with weight distribution), is not the MAC center, and is not the datum.

reference.text: The CG is a point at which the aircraft would balance if it were possible to suspend it at that point.

questions.question: Why is the forward CG limit often established based on an aircraft's landing characteristics?
questions.correct_answer: Exceeding the forward CG limit during landing may result in excessive loads on the nosewheel and higher stalling speeds
distractors: A forward CG improves landing performance by increasing approach speed
The forward CG limit determines the maximum landing weight of the aircraft
A forward CG during landing reduces elevator effectiveness during cruise flight
questions.explanation: The chapter states the forward CG limit is determined by landing characteristics, and exceeding it may cause excessive nosewheel loads, nose-over tendency in tailwheel aircraft, decreased performance, higher stalling speeds, and higher control forces. The distractors describe incorrect relationships between forward CG and landing.

reference.text: The forward CG limit is often established at a location that is determined by the landing characteristics of an aircraft. During landing, one of the most critical phases of flight, exceeding the forward CG limit may result in excessive loads on the nosewheel, a tendency to nose over on tailwheel type airplanes, decreased performance, higher stalling speeds, and higher control forces.

questions.question: Which undesirable characteristic may result from a CG located aft of the allowable range?
questions.correct_answer: Violent stall characteristics and very light control forces
distractors: Excessive nose-down tendency during takeoff
Increased structural loads on the nosewheel during landing
Difficulty raising the nose for landing flare
questions.explanation: The chapter lists extreme control difficulty, violent stall characteristics, and very light control forces as effects of an aft CG. The distractors describe forward CG effects: nose-heavy takeoff difficulty, nosewheel loads, and inability to flare are all associated with a forward CG, not aft.

reference.text: other undesirable effects caused by a CG location aft of the allowable range may include extreme control difficulty, violent stall characteristics, and very light control forces which make it easy to overstress an aircraft inadvertently.

questions.section: Balance, Stability, and Center of Gravity
questions.question: In an airplane, lateral unbalance can occur if:
questions.correct_answer: Fuel is mismanaged by supplying the engine(s) unevenly from tanks on one side of the airplane
distractors: Baggage is loaded too far aft in the baggage compartment
Heavy passengers are placed in the rear seats
Fuel is burned from wing tanks located very near the CG
questions.explanation: The chapter specifically identifies uneven fuel management from tanks on one side as the cause of lateral unbalance. Loading baggage aft or heavy passengers in rear seats affects longitudinal balance, not lateral. Fuel tanks near the CG have little effect on CG when burned.

reference.text: In an airplane, lateral unbalance occurs if the fuel load is mismanaged by supplying the engine(s) unevenly from tanks on one side of the airplane.

questions.section: Management of Weight and Balance Control
questions.question: Under 14 CFR part 91, what is required of the pilot in command regarding weight and balance?
questions.correct_answer: The PIC must comply with the operating limits, including weight and balance, in the approved AFM
distractors: The PIC must conduct weight and balance calculations prior to each flight as specifically required by Part 91
The PIC must have the aircraft weighed every 36 calendar months
The PIC must obtain a weight and balance sign-off from a mechanic before each flight
questions.explanation: The chapter states that while Part 91 does not specifically require weight and balance calculations before each flight, section 91.9 requires the PIC to comply with operating limits in the approved AFM, which include weight and balance. The 36-month weighing requirement applies to Part 125 and Part 135 operations, not Part 91.

reference.text: While there are no specified requirements for a pilot operating under 14 CFR part 91 to conduct weight and balance calculations prior to each flight, 14 CFR part 91, section 91.9 requires the pilot in command (PIC) to comply with the operating limits in the approved AFM. These limits include the weight and balance of the aircraft.

questions.question: In weight and balance terminology, the 'arm' is defined as:
questions.correct_answer: The horizontal distance in inches from the reference datum line to the CG of an item
distractors: The weight of an item multiplied by its distance from the datum
The maximum weight the floor can sustain per square inch or foot
The distance between the forward and aft CG limits
questions.explanation: The chapter defines arm as the horizontal distance from the datum to the CG of an item. The first distractor defines moment, the second defines floor load limit, and the third defines CG range.

reference.text: Arm (moment arm)—the horizontal distance in inches from the reference datum line to the CG of an item.

questions.section: Principles of Weight and Balance Computations
questions.question: How is the moment of an item calculated?
questions.correct_answer: By multiplying the weight of the item by its arm
distractors: By dividing the weight by the arm
By adding the arm to the total weight
By subtracting the datum distance from the station number
questions.explanation: The chapter states that moment is the product of weight multiplied by arm. Dividing weight by arm, adding arm to weight, or subtracting distances do not produce a moment.

reference.text: If the weight of any object or component is multiplied by the distance from the datum (arm), the product is the moment.

questions.question: What is the standard weight of aviation gasoline per U.S. gallon?
distractors: 6.8 lb/US gal
7.5 lb/US gal
8.35 lb/US gal
questions.explanation: The chapter lists standard weights: gasoline at 6 lb/gal, Jet A at 6.8 lb/gal, oil at 7.5 lb/gal, and water at 8.35 lb/gal. The distractors correspond to other substances.

questions.question: Useful load is defined as the weight of:
questions.correct_answer: The pilot, copilot, passengers, baggage, usable fuel, and drainable oil
distractors: The airframe, engines, and all permanently installed operating equipment
The maximum weight exclusive of usable fuel
Only the expendable part of the aircraft's load, including usable fuel
questions.explanation: The chapter defines useful load as the weight of the pilot, copilot, passengers, baggage, usable fuel, and drainable oil. The first distractor describes standard empty weight, the second describes maximum zero fuel weight, and the third incorrectly limits useful load to only expendable items (fuel and oil), excluding the pilot, passengers, and baggage.

reference.text: Useful load—the weight of the pilot, copilot, passengers, baggage, usable fuel, and drainable oil.

questions.question: Under GAMA standardization, basic empty weight consists of:
questions.correct_answer: The standard empty weight plus the weight of optional and special equipment that have been installed
distractors: The airframe weight plus engine weight and usable fuel only
The maximum takeoff weight minus the useful load
The aircraft weight with full fuel but no passengers or baggage
questions.explanation: The chapter defines basic empty weight (GAMA) as standard empty weight plus optional and special equipment. Standard empty weight includes the airframe, engines, fixed ballast, hydraulic fluid, unusable fuel, and full engine oil. The distractors incorrectly include usable fuel or describe unrelated calculations.

reference.text: Basic empty weight (GAMA)—the standard empty weight plus the weight of optional and special equipment that have been installed.

questions.section: Determining Loaded Weight and CG — Computational Method
questions.question: When using the computational method, how is the CG location of a loaded aircraft determined?
questions.correct_answer: By dividing the total moment by the total weight
distractors: By multiplying the total weight by the total moment
By subtracting the empty weight CG from the loaded weight
By dividing the total weight by the total moment
questions.explanation: The chapter's computational method states: list weights and moments, find totals, then divide total moment by total weight to find CG. Multiplying weight by moment or dividing weight by moment do not yield CG location.

reference.text: To determine the CG, divide the total moment by the total weight.

questions.question: Which set of environmental conditions may require a reduction in aircraft weight before flight is attempted, even if the aircraft is certified for maximum gross takeoff weight?
questions.correct_answer: High elevation, high temperature, and high humidity
distractors: Low elevation, low temperature, and low humidity
Sea level pressure, standard temperature, and clear skies
Cold temperatures, dry air, and calm winds
questions.explanation: The chapter identifies high elevations, high temperatures, and high humidity (high density altitudes) as conditions that may require weight reduction. The distractors all describe favorable density altitude conditions that would not typically require weight reduction.

reference.text: Conditions that affect takeoff and climb performance, such as high elevations, high temperatures, and high humidity (high density altitudes), may require a reduction in weight before flight is attempted.

questions.section: Shifting, Adding, and Removing Weight — Weight Shifting
questions.question: When weight is shifted from one location to another within an aircraft, what happens to the total weight and total moments?
questions.correct_answer: The total weight remains unchanged, but the total moments change in proportion to the distance the weight is moved
distractors: Both the total weight and total moments remain unchanged
The total weight changes proportionally to the distance the weight is moved
The total moments remain unchanged, but the total weight changes
questions.explanation: The chapter states that when weight is shifted, total weight is unchanged, but total moments change in proportion to the direction and distance the weight is moved. The distractors incorrectly claim moments stay the same, weight changes, or both remain unchanged.

reference.text: When weight is shifted from one location to another, the total weight of the aircraft is unchanged. The total moments, however, do change in relation and proportion to the direction and distance the weight is moved.

questions.section: Shifting, Adding, and Removing Weight — Weight Addition or Removal
questions.question: When weight is added to an aircraft at a known station, how is the change in CG (∆CG) calculated?
questions.correct_answer: Divide the added weight by the new total weight, then multiply by the distance between the added weight and the old CG
distractors: Divide the added weight by the distance between the weight and the old CG
Multiply the added weight by the new total weight, then divide by the distance
Subtract the old CG from the added weight's station and divide by the total weight
questions.explanation: The chapter presents the formula: Added weight / New total weight = ∆CG / Distance between weight and old CG. Rearranging: ∆CG = (Added weight / New total weight) × Distance. The distractors do not match this proportional relationship.

reference.text: Added weight / New total weight = ∆CG / Distance between weight and old CG

questions.question: A restricted forward CG limit is specified in order to assure that:
questions.correct_answer: Sufficient elevator/control deflection is available at minimum airspeed
distractors: The aircraft can rotate earlier during the takeoff roll
The stall speed is minimized for approach
The structural load on the tailwheel is reduced
questions.explanation: The chapter states the forward CG limit is restricted to assure sufficient elevator/control deflection at minimum airspeed. A forward CG makes rotation harder, not earlier; it increases stall speed rather than minimizing it; and it affects nosewheel loads, not tailwheel loads.

reference.text: A restricted forward CG limit is also specified to assure that sufficient elevator/control deflection is available at minimum airspeed.

questions.question: Maximum zero fuel weight (GAMA) is defined as:
questions.correct_answer: The maximum weight exclusive of usable fuel
distractors: The maximum allowable weight for takeoff
The greatest weight an aircraft is normally allowed to have at landing
The weight of the aircraft with no fuel on board, including unusable fuel
questions.explanation: The chapter defines maximum zero fuel weight as the maximum weight exclusive of usable fuel. The distractors define maximum takeoff weight, maximum landing weight, or describe a state rather than a maximum limit.

reference.text: Maximum zero fuel weight (GAMA)—the maximum weight, exclusive of usable fuel.
